title: Biophysical Modeling
text:
Green anole range


Code
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it requires manual interaction
## to define the green anole's range using the `mapedit` package. The resulting 
## range points are saved as an RDS file for later use.

caro_occ_data <- read.csv("raw_data/anolis_carolinensis_inat_obs.csv")

# round coordinates and remove observations with low positional accuracy
caro_occ_data <- caro_occ_data |>
  mutate(
    lat = round(latitude, 1), lon = round(longitude, 1),
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(positional_accuracy) & positional_accuracy <= 1000
  ) |>
  group_by(lon, lat) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n > 2) |>
  select(lon, lat)

# filter data to native range of green anole
caro_occ_data <- caro_occ_data |>
  filter(
    lon > -110 & lon < -70, lat > 22.5 & lat < 37.5
  )

# remove outliers based on distance to other observations
caro_occ_data$is_outlier <- apply(
  caro_occ_data[, c("lon", "lat")], 1, function(x) {
    distances <- geosphere::distm(
      x,
      caro_occ_data[, c("lon", "lat")],
      fun = distHaversine
    )
    # if there are fewer than 3 observations within 50 km, mark as outlier
    if (length(distances) > 0 && sum(distances < 50000) < 3) {
      1
    } else {
      0
    }
  }
)

# save processed occurrence data
saveRDS(caro_occ_data, "data/caro_occ_data.rds")

# transform into a spatial object
caro_occ_sf <- st_as_sf(
  caro_occ_data[caro_occ_data$is_outlier == 0, ],
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)

# manually draw map around range
mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE)
caro_range_sf <- editMap(mapview(caro_occ_sf))

# transform into a polygon object
caro_range_sf <- st_as_sf(caro_range_sf$finished)

# filter data to only include points within the continental US
caro_range_sf <- st_intersection(
  caro_range_sf,
  ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
    filter(admin == "United States of America") |>
    st_crop(xmin = -125, xmax = -65, ymin = 20, ymax = 50)
)

# generate a grid of points within the range polygon
grid <- st_make_grid(caro_range_sf, cellsize = 0.1, square = TRUE)
caro_range_points <- grid[st_intersects(grid, caro_range_sf, sparse = FALSE)]
caro_range_points <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(caro_range_points))
caro_range_points <- caro_range_points |>
  rename(lon = X, lat = Y) |>
  mutate(
    lon = round(lon, 1), lat = round(lat, 1)
  ) |>
  distinct() |>
  select(lon, lat)

# save caro range points
saveRDS(caro_range_points, "data/caro_range_points.rds")

Ecological data


Code
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it requires downloading large
## datasets. The resulting ecological data is saved as an RDS file
## for later use.

# get polygon for the continental US
continental_us_polygon <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(admin == "United States of America") |>
  st_crop(
    xmin = min(caro_range_points$lon) - 2,
    xmax = max(caro_range_points$lon) + 2,
    ymin = min(caro_range_points$lat) - 2,
    ymax = max(caro_range_points$lat) + 2
  ) |>
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

# download 30s rasters for tree cover, wetland and mangrove
tree_cover_rast <- geodata::landcover(
  var = "trees", path = "raw_data/landuse"
)
wetland_rast <- geodata::landcover(
  var = "wetland", path = "raw_data/landuse"
)
mangrove_rast <- geodata::landcover(
  var = "mangroves", path = "raw_data/landuse"
)
vegetation_rast <- tree_cover_rast + wetland_rast + mangrove_rast

# crop and summarize vegetation rasters
vegetation_rast_us <- terra::crop(vegetation_rast, continental_us_polygon)
vegetation_rast_us <- terra::aggregate(vegetation_rast_us, fact = 12, fun = "mean") # nolint

# rdownload and process minimum temperature data
tmin_rast <- geodata::worldclim_global(
  var = "tmin", res = 0.5, path = "raw_data/wc2.1_30s_tmin"
)
tmin_files <- list.files("raw_data/wc2.1_30s_tmin", full.names = TRUE)
tmin_rast_list <- list()
for (i in seq_along(tmin_files)) {
  rast <- terra::rast(tmin_files[i])
  rast_us <- terra::crop(rast, continental_us_polygon)
  rast_us <- terra::aggregate(rast_us, fact = 12, fun = mean)
  tmin_rast_list <- append(tmin_rast_list, rast_us)
}

# read and process maximum temperature data
tmax_rast <- geodata::worldclim_global(
  var = "tmax", res = 0.5, path = "raw_data/wc2.1_30s_tmax"
)
tmax_files <- list.files("raw_data/wc2.1_30s_tmax", full.names = TRUE)
tmax_rast_list <- list()
for (i in seq_along(tmax_files)) {
  rast <- terra::rast(tmax_files[i])
  rast_us <- terra::crop(rast, continental_us_polygon)
  rast_us <- terra::aggregate(rast_us, fact = 12, fun = mean)
  tmax_rast_list <- append(tmax_rast_list, rast_us)
}

# combine all rasters into a single data frame
eco_rast_list <- c(vegetation_rast_us, tmin_rast_list, tmax_rast_list)
eco_df <- as.data.frame(eco_rast_list, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(eco_df) <- c("lon", "lat", "veg", paste0("tmin_", 1:12), paste0("tmax_", 1:12)) # nolint
eco_df$lon <- round(eco_df$lon, 1)
eco_df$lat <- round(eco_df$lat, 1)

# get elevation raster
elevation <- geodata::elevation_30s(
  lon = eco_df$lon,
  lat = eco_df$lat,
  path = "raw_data/elevation",
  country = "USA"
)
elevation <- terra::crop(elevation, continental_us_polygon)
elevation_df <- as.data.frame(elevation, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("lon", "lat", "elevation")) |>
  mutate(lat = round(lat, 1), lon = round(lon, 1)) |>
  group_by(lon, lat) |>
  summarise(elevation = mean(elevation, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# merge data
elevation_df <- merge(
  elevation_df,
  caro_range_points |> mutate(present = 1),
  by = c("lon", "lat"),
  all.x = TRUE
)
elevation_df$present[is.na(elevation_df$present)] <- 0

# combine all rasters into a single data frame
eco_df <- merge(eco_df, elevation_df, by = c("lon", "lat"), all.x = TRUE)
eco_df <- eco_df |> filter(!is.na(elevation))

# pivot longer for temperature data
eco_df <- eco_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(starts_with("tmin_"), starts_with("tmax_")),
    names_to = c("temp_type", "month"),
    names_pattern = "(tmin|tmax)_(\\d+)",
    values_to = "temp"
  ) |>
  mutate(month = as.integer(month)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = temp_type,
    values_from = temp
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = c(tmin, tmax))

# merge with caro range points to indicate presence/absence
eco_df <- merge(
  eco_df,
  caro_range_points |> mutate(present = 1),
  by = c("lon", "lat"),
  all.x = TRUE
)
eco_df$present[is.na(eco_df$present)] <- 0

# save final ecological data
saveRDS(eco_df, "data/eco_data.rds")



Physiological & Behavioral ThresholdsVegetation CoverMinimum Annual Temperature


In the plot below, we visualize how the green anole’s range is distributed across different temperature thresholds imposed by the physiology and behavior of the species. The thresholds are defined as follows:

Hard Threshold: Minimum annual temperature below 0°C, which is lethal for the species.
Soft Threshold: Minimum annual temperature between 0°C and 5.35°C, which is the lowest ever empirically estimated CTmin.
Behavioral Threshold: Minimum annual temperature between 5.35°C and 6.6°C, which is the temperature at which there is < 10% of observing green anoles perching at night based on our surveys.



Code
eco_data <- readRDS("data/eco_data.rds")

# define temp thresholds
thresh1 <- 0
thresh2 <- 5.35
thresh3 <- 6.6

eco_data |>
  group_by(lon, lat, present) |>
  summarise(
    min_temp = min(tmin, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    buckets = case_when(
      min_temp < thresh1 ~ "hard_thresh",
      min_temp >= thresh1 & min_temp < thresh2 ~ "soft_thresh",
      min_temp >= thresh2 & min_temp < thresh3 ~ "behavioral_thresh",
      TRUE ~ "rest_of_range"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    buckets = factor(
      buckets,
      levels = c(
        "hard_thresh",
        "soft_thresh",
        "behavioral_thresh",
        "rest_of_range"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = buckets)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_contour(
    aes(z = present),
    color = "white", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "hard_thresh" = "darkblue",
      "soft_thresh" = "steelblue",
      "behavioral_thresh" = "skyblue",
      "rest_of_range" = "gray"
    ),
    name = "Temperature\nThresholds",
    labels = c(
      "Hard Threshold (< 0°C)",
      "Soft Threshold (0-5.35°C)",
      "Behavioral Threshold (5.35-6.6°C)",
      "Rest of Range (> 6.6°C)"
    ),
    guide = guide_legend(
      ncol = 2
    )
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(25, 37.5)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-100, -75, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "°W"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(25, 37.5, by = 2.5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "°N"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA),
    axis.ticks = element_line(),

Biophysical Modeling
text:
Biophysical Modeling


Code
# define physical constants
k <- 0.05 # thermal conductivity of leaf litter (W m^-1 K^-1)
rho <- 150 # bulk density of leaf litter (kg m^-3)
cp <- 2500 # specific heat capacity of leaf litter (J kg^-1 K^-1)
cc <- 0.007 # canopy cooling coefficient (W m^-2)
srh <- 0.02 # surface radiative heat flux coefficient (C / W m^-2 K^-1)
ecc <- 0.0167 # earth orbit eccentricity
spo <- 1.36 # extraterrestial solar radiation (kW m^-2)
atc <- 0.83 # atmospheric transmissivity coefficient (unitless)

# calculate derived physical constants
diff_sec <- k / (rho * cp) # thermal diffusivity of leaf litter (m^2 s^-1)
diff_hour <- diff_sec * 3600 # thermal diffusivity of leaf litter (m^2 h^-1)
omega <- 2 * pi / 24 # angular frequency of diurnal temperature cycle (rad h^-1)
damping_depth <- sqrt((2 * diff_hour) / omega) # damping depth (m)

# define list of heights and depths of interest
zs <- c(seq(-0.2, -0.01, by = 0.01), 0, 1.8, 2.2, 3)




Code
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it requires significant computation time. 
## The resulting microclimate data is saved as an RDS file for later use.

eco_df <- eco_data

# define function to calculate solar radiation profile
get_solar_rad_profile <- function(lat, elev, doy, solar_noon) {
  hours <- 0:23
  elon <- (2 * pi / 365) * (doy - 80) + 2 * ecc * (sin(2 * pi / 365 * doy) - sin(2 * pi / 365 * 80)) # nolint
  dec_ang <- asin(0.3879672 * sin(elon))
  p_a <- 101.3 * exp(-elev / 8200)
  geo_lat <- lat * (pi / 180)
  sin_alt_ang <- sin(geo_lat) * sin(dec_ang) + cos(geo_lat) * cos(dec_ang) * outer(solar_noon, hours, function(s, h) cos(0.2618 * (h - s))) # nolint
  m_a <- p_a / (101.3 * (1 / sin_alt_ang))
  solar_rad <- spo * atc ^ m_a * sin_alt_ang
  solar_rad[solar_rad < 0] <- 0
  drop(solar_rad * 1000)
}

# define function to calculate air temperature profile
get_air_temp_profile <- function(tmax, tmin) {
  w <- pi / 12
  gamma <- 0.44 - 0.46 * sin(0.9 + w * (0:23)) + 0.11 * sin(0.9 + 2 * w * (0:23)) # nolint
  drop(outer(tmax, gamma) + outer(tmin, 1 - gamma))
}

# define function to correct air temperature profile from canopy cooling
correct_air_temp_profile <- function(
    air_temp_profile, cc = 0.007, solar_rad_profile, veg_cover) {
  is_vec <- is.vector(air_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
    solar_rad_profile <- matrix(solar_rad_profile, nrow = 1)
  }
  result <- air_temp_profile - sweep(cc * solar_rad_profile, 1, veg_cover, "*")
  if (is_vec) drop(result) else result
}

# define function to calculate surface temperature profile
get_surf_temp_profile <- function(
    air_temp_profile, solar_rad_profile, srh = 0.02, veg_cover) {
  is_vec <- is.vector(air_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
    solar_rad_profile <- matrix(solar_rad_profile, nrow = 1)
  }
  result <- air_temp_profile + sweep(srh * solar_rad_profile, 1, 1 - veg_cover, "*") # nolint
  if (is_vec) drop(result) else result
}

get_z_temp_profile <- function(
  z_list, surf_temp_profile, air_temp_profile, damping_depth, ref_height = 1.8
) {

  # check if the input profiles are vectors or matrices
  is_vec <- is.vector(surf_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    surf_temp_profile <- matrix(surf_temp_profile, nrow = 1)
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
  }

  # define hours and extended hours for interpolation
  hours <- 0:23
  surf_temp_mean <- rowMeans(surf_temp_profile)
  extended_hours <- c(hours - 24, hours, hours + 24)

  # calculate temperature profiles at different heights and depths
  z_temp_profiles <- lapply(z_list, function(z) {
    if (z == 0) {
      surf_temp_profile
    } else if (z == ref_height) {
      air_temp_profile
    } else if (z > 0) {
      a <- log((z + 0.01) / 0.01) / log((ref_height + 0.01) / 0.01)
      surf_temp_profile - (surf_temp_profile - air_temp_profile) * a
    } else {
      damp_ratio <- exp(-abs(z) / damping_depth)
      phase_lag <- (abs(z) / damping_depth) * (24 / (2 * pi))
      xout <- hours - phase_lag
      idx <- findInterval(xout, extended_hours)
      w <- (xout - extended_hours[idx]) / (extended_hours[idx + 1] - extended_hours[idx]) # nolint
      ext_surf <- cbind(surf_temp_profile, surf_temp_profile, surf_temp_profile)
      shifted_temp <- sweep(ext_surf[, idx],     2, 1 - w, "*") + sweep(ext_surf[, idx + 1], 2, w, "*") # nolint
      surf_temp_mean + (shifted_temp - surf_temp_mean) * damp_ratio
    }
  })

  # combine the temperature profiles into a matrix
  names(z_temp_profiles) <- z_list
  if (is_vec) z_temp_profiles <- lapply(z_temp_profiles, drop)
  z_temp_profiles

}

# get solar noon time for each point in eco_df
eco_df$solar_noon <- mapply(
  TrenchR::solar_noon,
  lon = eco_df$lon,
  doy = eco_df$month * 30 - 15
)

# calculate air temperature profile for every point in eco_df
air_temp_prof <- get_air_temp_profile(
  tmax = eco_df$tmax,
  tmin = eco_df$tmin
)

# calculate solar radiation profile for every point in eco_df
solar_rad_prof <- get_solar_rad_profile(
  lat = eco_df$lat,
  elev = eco_df$elevation,
  doy = eco_df$month * 30 - 15,
  solar_noon = eco_df$solar_noon
)

# calculate corrected air temperature profile for every point in eco_df
air_temp_prof_corrected <- correct_air_temp_profile(
  air_temp_profile = air_temp_prof,
  solar_rad_profile = solar_rad_prof,
  veg_cover = eco_df$veg
)

# calculate surface temperature profile for every point in eco_df
surf_temp_prof <- get_surf_temp_profile(
  air_temp_profile = air_temp_prof_corrected,
  solar_rad_profile = solar_rad_prof,
  veg_cover = eco_df$veg
)

# calculate temperature profiles at different heights and depths for every point in eco_df # nolint
zs_temp_profiles <- get_z_temp_profile(
  z_list = zs,
  surf_temp_profile = surf_temp_prof,
  air_temp_profile = air_temp_prof_corrected,
  damping_depth = damping_depth
)

# summarize zs temperature profiles into a data frame
microclimate_temps <- Map(
  function(z_temp, z_val) {
    data.frame(
      lon = eco_df$lon,
      lat = eco_df$lat,
      elev = eco_df$elevation,
      veg = eco_df$veg,
      presence = eco_df$present,
      z                = z_val,
      min_temp         # calculate temperature profiles at different heights and depths for every point in eco_df # nolint
zs_temp_profiles <- get_z_temp_profile(
  z_list = zs,
  surf_temp_profile = surf_temp_prof,
  air_temp_profile = air_temp_prof_corrected,
  damping_depth = damping_depth
)= do.call(pmin, as.data.frame(z_temp)),
      hours_below_0C   = rowSums(z_temp < 0),
      hours_below_6.8C = rowSums(z_temp < 6.8)
    )
  },
  zs_temp_profiles, zs
) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  group_by(lon, lat, elev, veg, presence, z) |>
  summarise(
    min_annual_temp   = min(min_temp),
    hours_below_0C    = sum(hours_below_0C),
    hours_below_ctmin = sum(hours_below_6.8C),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# save zs_temp_profiles
saveRDS(microclimate_temps, "data/microclimate_temps.rds")

microclimate_temps <- readRDS("data/microclimate_temps.rds")

summarized_microclimates <- microclimate_temps |>
  filter(presence == 1) |>
  group_by(lat, z) |>
  summarise(
    mean_min_temp = mean(min_annual_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_min_temp = max(min_annual_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_min_temp = min(min_annual_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(as.character(z) %in% c("-0.05", "2.2")) |>

title: Time for Space Analysis of Retreating Temperatures
text:
Code
# packages
library(tidyverse)
library(NicheMapR)
library(kableExtra)

# options
options(
  dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE,
  knitr.table.html.attr = "quarto-disable-processing=true"
)



Overview
The goal of this analysis is to estimate the threshold temperature at which Green Anoles (Anolis carolinensis) retreat to the leaf litter and are no longer observed in the tree canopy. To determine this threshold, we will combine field survey and iButton-based temperature data and later statistically analyze the relationship between temperature and both presence and abundance of Green Anoles.


Data Processing
Below we first read in the survey and iButton data. Both of these data have been previously processed to be compatible with subsequent analysis and each other.


Code
survey <- readRDS("data/sleepy-lizard-survey-data.rds")
ibutton <- readRDS("data/ibutton-data.rds")

as_tibble(survey)


# A tibble: 315 × 8

10  2025   268  1241     NA        NA        1224    1298              5
# ℹ 305 more rows


Code
as_tibble(ibutton)


# A tibble: 420,812 × 7
   location    id  year   doy   mod  temp microhabitat
   <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       
 1 ATL          1    24   355   800  13   leaflitter  
 2 ATL          1    24   355   830  13.5 leaflitter  
 3 ATL          1    24   355   860  13.5 leaflitter  
 4 ATL          1    24   355   890  14   leaflitter  
 5 ATL          1    24   355   920  13.5 leaflitter  
 6 ATL          1    24   355   950  13.5 leaflitter  
 7 ATL          1    24   355   980  13   leaflitter  
 8 ATL          1    24   355  1010  12.5 leaflitter  
 9 ATL          1    24   355  1040  12.5 leaflitter  
10 ATL          1    24   355  1070  12   leaflitter  
# ℹ 420,802 more rows


The dataset structure is as follows:

In survey, each row corresponds to a unique lizard observation. Some rows are left completely as NA indicating that no lizards were observed during that survey. It contains the following columns:

year: numeric year of the survey.
doy: numeric day of year of the survey.
mod: numeric minute of the day in which each observation occured.
air_temp: numeric air temperature in degrees Celsius at the time of the observation.
body_temp: numeric body temperature of the lizard in degrees Celsius at the time of the observation.
start_mod & end_mod: numeric start and end time of the survey in minutes since midnight
n_participants: numeric number of participants in the survey.

In ibutton, each row corresponds to a unique temperature observation from an iButton data logger. It contains the following columns:

location: character location where the iButton was deployed. Each value corresponds to a unique city including ATL, GNV, MIA, ORL, PSL.
id: numeric unique identifier for each iButton within each location.
year, doy, mod: same as in survey.
microhabitat: character microhabitat in which the iButton was deployed including leaflitter, branch.


Next we filter the iButton data to match the survey data and combine the two datasets. The resulting dataset contains the mean temperature for each microhabitat during each survey. In this case, we only use data from ATL to match the survey data, but we will use the complete dataset for other analyses.



Code for Processing Survey and iButton Data

# filter iButton data to match survey data
ibutton_survey <- ibutton |>
  filter(location == "ATL") |>
  mutate(year = year + 2000) |> # resolve year formatting issue
  filter(year >= min(survey$year) & year <= max(survey$year)) |>
  filter(paste(year, doy) %in% paste(survey$year, survey$doy)) |>
  left_join(
    survey |>
      select(year, doy, start_mod, end_mod) |>
      unique(),
    by = c("year", "doy")
  ) |>
  # one survey went past midnight, so we cap end_mod at 1440 (24 hours)
  mutate(end_mod = ifelse(end_mod > 1440, 1440, end_mod)) |>
  filter(mod >= start_mod & mod <= end_mod) |>
  group_by(year, doy, microhabitat) |>
  filter(temp > -10) |> # remove erroneous iButton readings
  summarise(
    mean_temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = microhabitat,
    values_from = mean_temp
  ) |>
  rename(
    branch_temp = branch,
    litter_temp = leaflitter
  )

# combine survey and iButton data
survey_ibutton <- survey |> left_join(ibutton_survey, by = c("year", "doy"))


Below we visualize provide a few visualizations of the combined dataset

Temperature DataPresence and AbundanceAmbient-Body Temperature Relationship


From the plot below, we can see that minimum temperatures in the leaf litter are consistently warmer than those in branches.


Code
theme_set(
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.line = element_line(),
      axis.ticks = element_line(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.05)
    )
)

ibutton |>
  filter(temp > -10) |>
  filter(year > 24) |>
  filter(!(year == 25 & doy < 200)) |>
  mutate(
    continuous_doy = ifelse(year == 26, doy + 365, doy)
  ) |>
  filter(location == "ATL") |>
  group_by(year, continuous_doy, microhabitat) |>
  summarise(
    min_temp = min(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_temp = max(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = continuous_doy, y = min_temp, color = microhabitat)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 365, color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(group = microhabitat), size = 1.25, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = microhabitat), method = "loess", linewidth = 1, se = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("forestgreen", "darkorange"),
    labels = c("Branch", "Leaf Litter")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(200, 600, 50),
    labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 365, x - 365, x)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of Year (Continuous)",
    y = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    color = "Microhabitat",
    subtitle = "Late 2025 to early 2026, ATL iButton Data"
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.spacing.x = unit(0, "lines")
  )


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'













Code
survey_ibutton |>
  group_by(year, doy, branch_temp, litter_temp) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    presence = ifelse(count > 1, 1, 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(continuous_doy = ifelse(year == 2026, doy + 365, doy)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(presence, count),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("presence", "count"),
      labels = c("Presence (0/1)", "Abundance (Count)")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = continuous_doy, y = value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 365, color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
    color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.5, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(200, 600, 50),
    labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 365, x - 365, x)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of Year (Continuous)",
    y = "Value",
    subtitle = "Late 2025 to early 2026, ATL Survey Data"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y")











Ambient and body temperatures are very strongly correlated and they pretty much follow a 1:1 relationship especially as ambient temperatures get colder.


Code
survey_ibutton |>
  filter(!is.na(body_temp)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = air_temp, y = body_temp)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.5, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", color = "darkgreen", fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Ambient Air Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Lizard Body Temperature (°C)",
    subtitle = "ATL Survey Data"
  )


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'














Estimating Retreating Temperature Threshold
In the following analyses, we model the relationship between branch temperature and lizard observation/abundance to identify temperature thresholds at which lizards retreat due to cold temperatures. We focus on branch temperature as a representative of the overall air temperature the lizard experiences in its “typical” habitat. We use two different models to estimate these thresholds: a binomial logistic regression and a Poisson regression. From each model fit, we then extract the most relevant temperature thresholds for lizard retreating behavior.

Observation Probability
First we visualize the relationship between branch temperature and the probability of observing at least one lizard during a survey.


Code
survey_ibutton |>
  group_by(year, doy, branch_temp, litter_temp) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    presence = ifelse(count > 1, 1, 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = branch_temp, y = presence)) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0, height = 0.01,
    color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.5, size = 3
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
    color = "darkgreen",
    fill = "forestgreen",
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean Branch Temp. (°C)",
    y = "Probability of Seeing at least ONE Lizard"
  )











Code
survey_ibutton_model_data <- survey_ibutton |>
  group_by(year, doy, branch_temp, litter_temp) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    presence = ifelse(count > 1, 1, 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

presence_model <- glm(
  presence ~ branch_temp,
  data = survey_ibutton_model_data,
  family = "binomial"
)
summary(presence_model)



Call:
glm(formula = presence ~ branch_temp, family = "binomial", data = survey_ibutton_model_data)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept)   -4.565      1.725  -2.647  0.00812 **
branch_temp    0.359      0.122   2.943  0.00325 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 45.475  on 32  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 25.862  on 31  degrees of freedom
  (1 observation deleted due to missingness)
AIC: 29.862

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


Code
# predict temperature thresholds
tibble(probability = c(0.5, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(
    logit = log(probability / (1 - probability)),
    temp_mean_est = round((logit - coef(presence_model)[1]) / coef(presence_model)[2], 2), # nolint
    temp_lower_est = round((logit - coef(presence_model)[1] - 1.96 * summary(presence_model)$coefficients[2, 2]) / coef(presence_model)[2], 2), # nolint
    temp_upper_est = round((logit - coef(presence_model)[1] + 1.96 * summary(presence_model)$coefficients[2, 2]) / coef(presence_model)[2], 2) # nolint
  ) |>
  select(probability, temp_mean_est, temp_lower_est, temp_upper_est) |>
  mutate(temp = paste(temp_mean_est, " (", temp_lower_est, " - ", temp_upper_est, ")", sep = "")) |>
  select(probability, temp) |>
  rename(
    `Probability of Observation` = probability,
    `Temp. (°C)` = temp
  ) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )



 
  
    Probability of Observation 
    Temp. (°C) 
  
 

  
    0.50 
    12.72 (12.05 - 13.38) 
  
  
    0.10 
    6.6 (5.93 - 7.26) 
  
  
    0.05 
    4.51 (3.85 - 5.18) 
  
  
    0.01 
    -0.08 (-0.75 - 0.58) 
  




The model, as expected, shows a significant positive effect of branch temperature on observation probability. The table above shows the estimated branch temperature thresholds at which we expect to observe lizards with different probabilities. For example, we expect to see at least one lizard during a survey 50% of the time when the branch temperature is around 12.72 °C, and we expect to see at least one lizard during a survey 10% of the time when the branch temperature is around 6.6 °C.


Abundance Probability
As before, we first visualize the relationship between branch temperature and the number of lizards observed during a survey.


Code
survey_ibutton |>
  group_by(year, doy, branch_temp, litter_temp) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    presence = ifelse(count > 1, 1, 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = branch_temp, y = count - 1)) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0, height = 0.01,
    color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.5, size = 3
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "poisson"),
    color = "darkgreen",
    fill = "forestgreen",
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean Branch Temp. (°C)",
    y = "Number of Lizards Observed"
  )











Code
abundance_model <- glm(
  count ~ branch_temp,
  data = survey_ibutton_model_data,
  family = "poisson"
)
summary(abundance_model)



Call:
glm(formula = count ~ branch_temp, family = "poisson", data = survey_ibutton_model_data)

Code
# predict temperature thresholds
tibble(counts = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)) |>
  mutate(
    log = log(counts),
    mean_temp_est = round((log - coef(abundance_model)[1]) / coef(abundance_model)[2], 2),
    max_temp_est = round((log - coef(abundance_model)[1] + 1.96 * summary(abundance_model)$coefficients[2, 2]) / coef(abundance_model)[2], 2),
    min_temp_est = round((log - coef(abundance_model)[1] - 1.96 * summary(abundance_model)$coefficients[2, 2]) / coef(abundance_model)[2], 2),
    temp = paste(mean_temp_est, " (", min_temp_est, " - ", max_temp_est, ")", sep = "")
  ) |>
  select(counts, temp) |>

    `Expected Count` = counts,

The abundance model shows an even stronger effect of branch temperature on the number of lizards observed during a survey. The table above shows the estimated branch temperature thresholds at which we expect to observe different numbers of lizards during a survey. For example, we expect to see an average of 1 lizard during a survey when the branch temperature is around 7.4 °C, and we expect to see an average of 5 lizards during a survey when the branch temperature is around 14.24 °C.
